newsitem.title: CHINA: Shanghai debates how to save Chinese brands.
newsitem.headline: Shanghai debates how to save Chinese brands.

text.p: Shanghai on Monday praised an electric tool company whose sales soared after it set up a joint venture, part of a debate over how to protect Chinese brands from foreign encroachment.

Shanghai Hitachi in 1995 produced 1.3 million electric tools with sales of 396 million yuan ($48 million), increases of 565 percent and 843 percent respectively over 1990, the first year of the joint venture, the Liberation Daily said on Monday.
Shanghai Electric Tool Factory held a 75 percent stake in the venture with Hitachi Corp and had retained its own "Dragon" brand for most of the products, it said.
"Recently a question attracting great discussion is how to protect national brands while attracting foreign investment," the newspaper said in a front-page editorial.
The success of the electric tool venture showed the two were not contradictory, it said.

But that is not how it looked to Zou Xianfu, general manager of Zhang Xiaoquan Knife Scissors Store, Shanghai's top seller of knives and scissors, with estimated 1996 sales of 30 million yuan, up from 24 million in 1995.

He declined an offer by German giant Zwilling J.A. Henckels AG to set up a joint venture in Shanghai to produce 500,000 pieces a year after the German side insisted it made only goods bearing the German brand name and not the Chinese name.

"We wanted to use the joint venture to raise the quality of our brand," Zou said in an interview on Monday. "If it made only German brand-name products, the quality of our brands would have remained at a low level. The technology gap is wide.
"Our brand is a precious asset handed down to us over several hundred years," he said. "We could not be responsible for giving it up."

In the window of Zou's main store in Shanghai's busiest shopping street is a 1956 inscription from Chairman Mao Zedong which reads: "The knives and scissors of Zhang Xiaoquan must be saved for 10,000 years."
The refusal of Zhang Xiaoquan became a cause celebre in the local and national media, which showered praise on the firm for its defence of a national brand.
But, snubbed by Zou, the German company took their offer to another state company, Shanghai Razor Company, which accepted.

The two are building a joint venture plant in the Pudong New Area of Shanghai that is due to start production late this year, with initial output of 500,000 pieces a year, a Shanghai Razor official said. The German side holds 70 percent.
"The joint venture will make knives costing from less than 70 yuan to more than 200," he said. "The cheaper ones will compete with Zhang Xiaoquan's products," he said.
"The German company is a world leader in its field, with a history of 256 years," he said.
In 1992, Shanghai Razor set up a joint venture with the Gillette Co, which produces both Gillette razors and its own "Flying Eagle" razor brand.

The joint venture in which Gillette has a controlling share pays Shanghai Razor each year 12 million yuan as a trademark fee and a percentage of sales of "Flying Eagle", amounting to about three million yuan a year.
